svg.text: Via-in-pad — why the 0.5 mm pitch decides the whole build
289 balls on a 17 × 17 grid at 0.5 mm pitch. The package choice was made to fit a 29 mm camera housing; this is the bill that choice presents to the fabricator.
A · DOG-BONE FANOUT
the conventional escape — it runs out after two rows
B · VIA-IN-PAD
filled and capped microvia inside every land
0.500 pitch
green: rows 1–2 escape by dog-bone
red: rows 3 and inward have nowhere to put the via land
0.20 mm mechanical drill
+ 2 × 0.075 mm annular ring
= 0.350 mm minimum via land
0.350 > 0.250 → will not fit
Rows 1 and 2 escape by dog-bone. Rows 3 to 9 have nowhere to go.
On a 17 × 17 grid that strands roughly 170 of the 289 balls.
capture pad 0.250 mm on L2, staggered second hop to L3
green: every land escapes, on any row
Ø0.100 mm laser drill
80 µm dielectric → 0.8 aspect ratio
copper filled, plated over, dimple ≤ 25 µm
0.100 < 0.250 → sits inside the land
The cost is real: VIPPO, laser drilling and sequential lamination roughly
double the bare-board price. Apply it only where the pitch demands it.
WHERE IT APPLIES, AND WHERE IT DOES NOT
LIFCL-40 289-csBGA — via-in-pad, mandatory.
0.5 mm pitch, 17 × 17 full grid. Nothing else reaches
the interior.
TPS62801/2 WCSP-6 — not needed.
0.35 mm pitch is finer, but all six balls are on the
perimeter of a 2 × 3 array, so every one of them escapes
outward on L1 at 0.075 mm. Finer pitch does not
automatically mean via-in-pad; a full grid does.
DDR3L 96-FBGA at 0.8 mm — dog-bone.
0.8 mm pitch leaves a 0.4 mm gap, which takes a 0.35 mm
via land with room to spare.
QFN thermal pads — vias, but a different spec.
Ø0.25 mm through vias on a 1.0 mm grid, tented from the
bottom. Filling is for solder-volume control, not for
flatness, so plugging is acceptable here where it is not
under the BGA.
Tell the fabricator which pads, not 'all'.
A blanket VIPPO note on a board with 900 vias is an
expensive way to ask for 289. Put the via-in-pad set on
its own layer in the fab package.
DFM CONSEQUENCES THAT FOLLOW
NSMD lands on the BGA, 0.25 mm copper.
Solder-mask-defined lands crack at the mask edge under a
rigid csBGA. Mask opening 0.325 mm.
Local fiducials, two per fine-pitch device.
1.0 mm copper, 2.0 mm mask clearance, diagonally
opposite. Three global fiducials on the board and two
more on the panel rail.
Stencil 0.100 mm, 1:1 apertures on the BGA.
Area ratio 0.63 at 0.25 mm round — go to a 0.27 mm
square-with-radius aperture to clear 0.66.
PANELISATION AND HANDLING
Tab-route, not V-score.
Components sit within 1.5 mm of three edges and V-scoring
puts a blade through that. Five 2.0 mm tabs per long edge,
three per short edge, perforated, 3 mm from any ceramic.
Orient MLCCs with their long axis parallel to the break line.
Depanel bending strains the board perpendicular to that
line. A capacitor lying across it takes the full strain
between its terminations; one lying along it takes almost
none.
2-up array, 5 mm rails, one board rotated 180°.
Copper balance across the panel is what keeps a 1.05 mm
ten-layer board flat enough for a 9.5 mm BGA.
TEST AND REWORK
No test points. Boundary scan instead.
There is no room for a bed of nails on 27 × 27 mm. JTAG
boundary scan covers the FPGA, the DDR3L interface and
every net that terminates on an FPGA ball — which is most
of them.
Tag-Connect pads, no header.
A 10-pad TC2050 footprint costs 5.5 × 3.0 mm of
bottom-side area and zero components.
Accept that the FPGA is not reworkable.
Filled microvias under a csBGA survive one reflow reliably
and two if you are lucky. Budget scrap rather than rework,
and say so in the assembly notes.
